tier_reason: PLDI 2023 paper compares flap against ocamlyacc and menhir (table and code backends) on six grammars. Benchmark code is public in the repo under benchmarks/ (e.g. benchmarks/json, benchmarks/csv, benchmarks/intexp; Core_bench harnesses with ocamlopt_flags -O3 in each dune file). The paper states the compiler (BER MetaOCaml N111, flambda) and CPU (Intel i9-12900K), so code, compiler, flags and CPU are all present.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: flap 'generates specialized token-free code that runs two to six times faster than ocamlyacc on a range of benchmarks.' Figure 11 throughput bar labels (MB/s): json flap=1359 vs ocamlyacc=236 (~5.8x, derived from page data) and vs menhir+code=326 (~4.2x, derived from page data); csv flap=323 vs ocamlyacc=70 (~4.6x, derived from page data); pgn flap=286 vs ocamlyacc=67 (~4.3x, derived from page data); ppm flap=104 vs ocamlyacc=16 (~6.5x, derived from page data); sexp flap=213 vs ocamlyacc=76 (~2.8x, derived from page data); arith flap=57 vs ocamlyacc=30 (~1.9x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: BER MetaOCaml N111 with flambda optimizations enabled; ocamlopt_flags -O3 in each benchmarks/*/dune file
corrections.workload: Six grammars benchmarked with Core_bench: Portable Game Notation (pgn, 6759 games), Netpbm PPM images (ppm), S-expressions (sexp), CSV (csv, Shafranovich RFC 4180 with mandatory CRLF), JSON (json), and a small arithmetic/comparison/binding/branching language (arith). Fig. 12 shows linear running time over input sizes up to about 2 MB (sexp, arith), 0.4 MB (csv), 40 kpixels (ppm), 4000 games (pgn) and 150 messages (json).
corrections.caveats: Baseline is ocamlyacc/menhir (OCaml-ecosystem yacc-family tools), not Bison/ANTLR/Boost.Spirit/nom directly, though ocamlyacc is architecturally the same class of tool as Bison; single-core, single-CPU-model microbenchmark; peer-reviewed at PLDI 2023 with a public Zenodo artifact (paper and README cite 10.5281/zenodo.7712770); project repo has had no commits since 2023-07-01.

notes: Figure 11 text is garbled in extraction; I decoded bar labels from PDF word positions and cross-checked them against the paper's inline flap/asp and flap/normalized ratios. The record's csv ocamlyacc value (76) is actually the menhir+table bar; ocamlyacc csv is 70. The record's Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.7824835 was not seen; the paper and README cite 10.5281/zenodo.7712770.

tier_reason: Paper (preprint submitted to Science of Computer Programming) compares the PAPAGENO parallel lexer+parser against a sequential Flex+Bison LALR(1) analyzer (Fig. 13). The Flex+Bison baseline code is public in the repo at test/benchmarks/bison_baselines/{json,lua}, alongside the PAPAGENO test harnesses in test/JSON and test/Lua. The paper states gcc 4.9.1, -O3 -march=native and the CPUs (quad Opteron 8378; Exynos 5 Octa).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Text (Sec. 6, 'Comparison with Flex and Bison'): the PAPAGENO-generated parallel lexer/parser shows 'a significant speedup with respect to the state-of-the-art of tool generated parsers, for all but the smallest test-bench files' on both server and mobile platforms. On the ARM platform the paper reports 'a speedup of up to 5.5x, as a combination of the parallel processing technique on multiple cores and the lesser computational requirements with respect to a classic LALR(1) parser.' Figure 13b (JSON, 16-core server) is a 3D surface plot whose speedup axis runs to 7; the text gives no exact peak value against Flex+Bison. The text's explicit 'maximum achieved speedup is 7x' refers to parallel lexing vs a sequential Flex lexer (Fig. 11a), not to the full Flex+Bison comparison.
corrections.workload: Lexing+AST-construction of real-world JSON files (2.7KiB-75MiB: online-shop shopping list, AdBlocker config, Gospel of John, Italian food-consumption stats, Google Books n-gram stats, UK CKAN index) and Lua files (7KiB-35MiB, built by concatenating files from LucasArts' Grim Fandango codebase), on a 16-core x86_64 Opteron server and a 4x Cortex-A15/4x Cortex-A7 ARM board.

notes: The default branch's last commit is 2015-04-20; repo pushed_at is 2015-09-11, which is probably a non-commit push. The record's 'roughly 7x' Fig. 13b figure was a chart-axis reading, so I reworded it to say the text gives no exact value. The rest of the record matches the paper.

tier_reason: The arXiv paper compares pika against ANTLR4 4.8-1 and Parboiled2 1.3.1 (Ryzen 1800X, JRE 13.0.2). It is an author-run preprint (arXiv comment: 'Submitted to ACM'), and I found no peer-reviewed venue. The repo contains only the Parboiled2 harness (src/test/java/pikaparser/Benchmark.java), with no ANTLR4 harness and no JVM flags. So this is first-party evidence with partial methodology: not A, not B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: JRE 13.0.2 (no JVM flags stated); baselines Parboiled2 1.3.1 and ANTLR4 4.8-1
corrections.caveats: Not a universal speed win: the same paper shows pika is 10-1000x slower than both baselines on the Java grammar. The repo's test suite (src/test/java/pikaparser/Benchmark.java) covers only the Parboiled2 comparison; no ANTLR4 harness is in the repo (only result plots under paper/), so the ANTLR4 numbers cannot be re-run from this codebase. The paper is an arXiv preprint ('Submitted to ACM'); no peer-reviewed publication was found, which keeps it at tier C. The expression-grammar win comes from ANTLR4/Parboiled2 superlinear scaling on very long (up to 4.8M-char) single expressions.

notes: The quoted numbers ('roughly the same speed', '10 times faster than ANTLR4', '1000 times faster than Parboiled2', 'up to 1000, 100 or 10 times slower') all appear in Sec. 4.3-4.4. The record's claim that the paper was published at SLE 2020 is not supported: arXiv and the README cite only the preprint, and one web search found no conference or journal version. DBLP was blocked by a bot wall.

tier_reason: The README's Performance section gives Criterion numbers against nom, peg, winnow, pest and chumsky. The harness is public (examples/paren_bench/benches/paren.rs) and the RUSTFLAGS and crate versions are stated. No CPU model or rustc version is given, so this is first-party evidence with partial methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: static-codegen backend (FastParse) 'beats pest, peg, nom, winnow, chumsky, and even serde_json on equal-work recognition benchmarks.' Criterion numbers: nested-parens depth 1024, MPL 2.26us vs nom 7.50us (~3.3x, derived from page data); depth 4096, MPL 9.23us vs nom 20.8us (~2.25x, derived from page data); flat-1024, MPL 2.11us vs nom 4.92us (~2.3x, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Micro-benchmarks, mostly recognition-only (bool result, no AST): nested/flat parenthesis matching (depth 1024/4096, flat-1024) vs nom/peg/winnow/pest/chumsky; JSON-subset recognition on json/canada/twitter/citm shapes vs peg (plus a token-queue tier vs pest and a reference tier vs serde_json Value); left-recursive-sum (lsum-64/256/1024) vs peg cache_left_rec.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark written and run by the sole maintainer, not independently reproduced; no CPU model or rustc version is stated (only RUSTFLAGS and crate versions). nom is compared only on the parenthesis benchmark. The serde_json comparison is not equal-work: the README itself says a fair direct comparison needs a Token-to-Value walker that is not yet shipped, and MPL's token-producing tier is slower than serde_json. pest beats MPL by 1.68x on canada-1024 in the token tier. Adoption is minimal (6 GitHub stars).

notes: The numbers match the README tables. The default branch's last commit is 2026-05-30; pushed_at 2026-07-25 comes from dependabot branches. The README's 'beats every comparator' claim is contradicted by its own canada-1024 token-tier row.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party timings for multi-threaded Rejit (sample/regexdna-multithread.cc) against the Benchmarks Game RE2 regex-dna program, and for jrep against GNU grep 2.14. The CPU (i5-2400) and engine commits are stated, but the compiler and flags are not (the repo SConstruct release mode only implies -O3). The RE2 side's program is external, so this is not A. It is first-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Benchmarks Game regex-dna, real time, Benchmarks Game RE2 program vs multi-threaded Rejit: 500KB 0.022s vs 0.011s (2.0x, derived from page data); 5MB 0.183s vs 0.087s (~2.1x, derived from page data); 50MB 1.629s vs 0.971s (~1.68x, derived from page data); 500MB 20.693s vs 11.594s (~1.78x, derived from page data). README: jrep (Rejit-powered grep) 'performs 1.68 times faster than gnu grep' on grep -R over linux-3.10.6 (0.622s vs 0.370s real). Single-threaded Rejit vs V8: 50MB 2.054s vs 1.246s (~1.65x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in README; repo SConstruct release mode adds -O3 (compiler and version unstated)
corrections.caveats: GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION, but the LICENCE file contains the full GNU GPL v3 text and the README says GPLv3. The RE2 comparison pits multi-threaded Rejit against the Benchmarks Game RE2 program; the README calls that program single-threaded yet links a u32q quad-core page, so thread-count parity is unclear. Compiler and flags are unstated. No commits since 2015; the benchmark numbers date from about 2013 (RE2 commit aa957b5e3374, Linux 3.10.6), and RE2 has been heavily optimized since. Rejit is described as a prototype and supports x86_64 only.

notes: The record's '~1.4x-1.8x across all sizes' was wrong: the README's own RE2 rows give 1.68x-2.1x. The tier drops from A to C because compiler and flags are missing and the benchmark is first-party. License GPL-3.0 is confirmed from the LICENCE file.
